prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology and active peptide forms of glucagon-like peptide-1 that led to incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B046 is the only candidate on which all six opening ballots agree on first place, and I think the agreement is earned on the merits rather than a product of coordination. It offers a complete arc from gut-hormone physiology (proglucagon processing, GLP-1 secretion and insulinotropic action in humans, identification of the biologically active truncated peptide) to a drug class with large randomized outcome trials, cardiovascular and renal benefit, and very broad patient impact. Maturity is high and timing is arguably pressing. Having listened to colleagues, I now think the cleanest configuration honours the discovery of the physiology and the active peptide: Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. I opened with Knudsen in the third slot, but the 3-person cap forces a choice, and five of six colleagues placed the physiological and peptide-identification contributions ahead of industrial analogue development.
statement.case_against: The attribution is genuinely untidy. Mojsov's priority on the active GLP-1(7-36) form is contested, Habener and other early contributors are outside the credited names, and omitting Knudsen leaves the translation to semaglutide and liraglutide unrecognised even though that is where much of the patient impact originates. A prize on physiology can be criticised as honouring the hormone biology while the therapeutic payoff was delivered by industry; conversely, a prize with Knudsen risks crowding out a basic discoverer. I cannot independently verify the priority disputes from the supplied evidence, and a single-part prize also leaves out strong second achievements such as CAR-T.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks B046 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, treating Knudsen's role as industrial engineering of the drug, and also supports B028 with June, Sadelain and Rosenberg as a strong second achievement.
responses.response: I now agree with the Drucker, Holst, Mojsov set and have moved Knudsen out of my proposal, although I do not regard her role as merely engineering: durable long-acting analogues were a genuine scientific achievement. I would qualify your inclusion of Rosenberg in B028. His contribution is adoptive cell transfer and early gene-engineered T cells rather than the CAR design itself, so a credit to June and Sadelain is cleaner, and the omission of Eshhar from the credited names still weakens the CAR-T case in my view.

responses.point: Perlmann places B029 (cGAS-STING; Chen and Barber) second, arguing the mechanism is clean and broadly important across infection, autoimmunity and cancer, though translation is still maturing.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual clarity of Chen's cGAS and cGAMP work and Barber's STING identification, but I rank it lower than you because the medical payoff is still prospective: no approved STING-directed drug exists, and Ishikawa's co-discovery of STING complicates a two-name credit. It is a strong future candidate, but compared with CAR-T therapies, which already produce durable remissions, I think the maturity gap is real. I would be open to hearing what human genetic evidence you consider decisive for timeliness.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks B007 (Krainer and Bennett, nusinersen) second as a clear link from splicing mechanism to a transformative RNA therapy, and proposes only June and Sadelain for CAR-T.
responses.response: I agree on the Krainer and Bennett pairing being coherent and the clinical effect in infants being dramatic, and I ranked it sixth mainly because other SMA therapies (gene replacement, small molecules) and the broader antisense platform complicate how a citation would be framed. I share your preference for limiting B028 to June and Sadelain, which fits the 3-person cap if paired with B046. Where I disagree is ordering: I see CAR-T as the broader new modality, but I would not resist B007 as a second part if the committee prefers an RNA-therapeutics theme.

responses.point: El Manira ranks B038 (optogenetics) second and B011 (unfolded protein response) third, valuing foundational impact on neuroscience and cell biology and lower on CAR-T.
responses.response: I take the breadth of optogenetics seriously, but with six credited names and a 3-person limit, any selection excludes decisive contributors such as Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck, and its impact is largely as a research tool rather than a medical treatment. On B011 we agree: Walter and Mori are a compact, very mature credit. My difference is that I would keep it as an alternative rather than a core part, because disease-level translation lags the conceptual impact.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks B028 second and B019 (imatinib) third, and notes that the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL fusion discoveries lie outside the credited set.
responses.response: I agree that B019 has a strong clinical case, but the attribution issue you raise is substantial: much of the foundational BCR-ABL biology predates and lies outside Druker, Lydon and Sawyers, and the Lasker award has already marked the trio. I rank it seventh for that reason, although the paradigm of targeted therapy is clearly important and recognition is not premature.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wishes to honour GLP-1 physiology or drug development, and whether Knudsen should displace Mojsov given the priority dispute.
Whether B046 alone is the right prize or should be paired with a second distinct achievement under the 3-person cap, which would require dropping one B046 name.
Resolution of the Eshhar omission for B028 and of Ishikawa's role for B029.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted ballots. I have about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann (dopamine neurons, Nurr1) and a postdoctoral link to Paul Greengard, but neither is a credited name on any shortlisted candidate; I flag these as background for transparency, not as recusal grounds.
